The View from SomewherePart II · Price levels across countries

Chapter 7

Countries that buy different goods

Web edition. Figure 7.3 is live: tick which countries buy which goods, draw a new economy, or change the elasticity, and the indexes and loop sums follow.

Here is a small invented example, small enough to do on the back of an envelope. Three countries, A, B and C, and ten goods. Every country buys six of the ten, and no country buys the same six as another. Figure 7.1 shows who buys what. Country A buys tea, rice, rye, cheese, salt and oats; country B buys rye, cheese, coffee, maize, salt and lamb; country C buys tea, rice, coffee, maize, salt and olives. Every pair shares three goods, and salt is the only good all three buy.

Give all three countries the same tastes. They have constant-elasticity preferences with σ=4, the same taste weight on each good in all three countries, and different prices. Then the exact price level Pc of each country exists, the true price index between countries j and k is log⁡Pk−log⁡Pj, and the three true indexes pass the circularity test by construction: around the triangle they sum to zero. Now do what a statistician with the actual data would do. Compare each pair on the goods the pair shares, with each country’s spending shares renormalized to sum to one on those goods, and use the Sato–Vartia index of Chapter 6. Call that the matched index. The numbers, in log points, are:

Pair Shared goods Matched index True index
A to B 3 0.310 −0.351
B to C 3 0.604 0.366
A to C 3 −0.065 0.016
Loop sum, A to B to C and back 0.978 0.000

The matched index says country B is 0.310 log points dearer than country A; the truth is that B is 0.351 cheaper. The sign is wrong. The three matched indexes fail the circularity test by almost a full log point. Nothing in this economy disagrees with anything: tastes are identical, one price level per country accounts for every true comparison. The failure comes entirely from comparing countries on different sets of goods.

We should say how this draw was made, because it is a dramatic one. The log prices come from a seeded script (figures/ch07_toy.py) with a standard deviation of 0.3, run once, with no hunting for a striking seed. But ten goods and three shared per pair is a far smaller economy than those of Section 7.6, where forty goods are spread over eight countries, though its overlap of a third is within their range. Figure 7.6 shows how large the loop sum typically is with forty goods.

This chapter finds out where the error comes from, which turns out to be a single number per country per pair, and then asks what that number does to the picture of Part I. It is the third research cycle of the project.

7.1What the matched index throws away

Take Chapter 6’s setting. Country c buys the goods in a set Gc, with expenditure shares sic=bicpic1−σPc1−σ,Pc1−σ=∑i∈Gcbicpic1−σ,i∈Gc,sic=bicpic1−σPc1−σ,Pc1−σ=∑i∈Gcbicpic1−σ,i∈Gc, where bic is a taste weight. Chapter 6 shows that on one common list of goods, the Sato–Vartia index equals log⁡Pk−log⁡Pj plus a taste term θjk that vanishes when tastes are identical.

Fix a pair j,k and let S=Gj∩Gk be the goods both buy. Define λcjk=∑i∈Ssic,c∈{j,k},λcjk=∑i∈Ssic,c∈{j,k}, the share of country c’s spending that falls on the goods in S. After renormalizing on S, country c’s shares are sic/λcjk, and these are exactly the shares of a CES country whose goods are only S. Its price level is PcS, defined by (PcS)1−σ=∑i∈Sbicpic1−σ=λcjkPc1−σ. The matched index is the Sato–Vartia index of these two sub-economies, so the identity of Chapter 6 applies to them: SVjkS=(log⁡PkS−log⁡PjS)+θjkS. Now take logs of (PcS)1−σ=λcjkPc1−σ: log⁡PcS=log⁡Pc−log⁡λcjkσ−1. Because λ<1 whenever goods are dropped, the log is negative and the sub-basket price level PcS lies above the true price level Pc. A country that drops goods looks dearer, by an amount that grows as the dropped goods account for more of its budget. In the example, B spends only 0.080 of its budget on the three goods it shares with A, and A spends 0.579 on them, so B’s price level is inflated by −log⁡λBAB/3=0.8426 and A’s by 0.1823. The difference, 0.6603, is how far the matched index sits above the truth on that edge, −0.3506+0.6603=0.3097, the table’s 0.310.

Substituting, the matched index is SVjkS=(log⁡Pk−log⁡Pj)−log⁡λkjk−log⁡λjjkσ−1+θjkS. The middle term is the problem. It has the form of a difference across the edge, but λkjk is not a property of country k. It is a property of the pair, because the set S changes with the pair. If every pair shared the same set S, then log⁡λc would be one number per country and its difference across an edge would be a coboundary, contributing nothing to any loop. That is why the experiment of Chapter 6, where every country had every good, found no trouble from this source. When the sets differ, the difference of log⁡λ does not telescope around a loop, and the matched index inherits an obstruction that has nothing to do with disagreement between countries.

The repair is to put the term back. Feenstra’s variety adjustment, in its spatial version, is (7.1)correctedjk=SVjkS+1σ−1(log⁡λkjk−log⁡λjjk)=(log⁡Pk−log⁡Pj)+θjkS. The second equality is the algebra above. The corrected index is the true difference in price levels plus a taste term, computed on the common goods. With identical tastes the taste term is zero, the corrected index equals log⁡Pk−log⁡Pj exactly, and so it passes the circularity test at every overlap. In the example the corrected indexes are −0.351, 0.366 and 0.016, equal to the truth to the third decimal, and their loop sum is zero to machine precision.

7.2The correction on one edge, and around a triangle

Figure 7.2 draws the edge from A to B. Each bar is a country’s whole budget. The dark part is spending on the three shared goods. The matched index sees only the dark part of each bar, rescaled to fill the bar. The correction is a function of how much of each bar was dark.

Now put the correction on every edge. Figure 7.3 shows the triangle with a number at each end of each edge: the λ for that country on that pair. Six numbers, one at each end of each edge, where a country has two numbers because it sits on two edges.

Three more points about the correction. The first is in the memo; the second and third we derived for this chapter.

Tastes. With tastes that differ across countries the corrected index is not the truth. By equation (7.1) it is the true index plus the taste term θjkS of Chapter 6, now computed on the common goods and with weights that depend on the pair. In the invented economy with a taste dispersion of 0.2 (a normal draw added to each log taste weight, also from the script) the corrected loop sum is 0.007 against a matched loop sum of 0.994. What remains is the taste obstruction of Chapter 6, nothing more, and the experiment below shows it stays that way.

The elasticity. The correction divides by σ−1. If the analyst uses σ′ in place of the true σ, then since the matched index itself does not use the elasticity, the corrected index misses the true one by (1σ′−1−1σ−1)(log⁡λkjk−log⁡λjjk). That is a pair-specific term again, so a wrong elasticity puts an obstruction back, equal to (1σ′−1−1σ−1) times the loop sum of the log⁡λ differences. In the invented economy that loop sum is −2.935, and with σ′=2 in place of 4 the corrected loop sum is 23×(−2.935)=−1.957, worse than the matched one. This follows from the derivation above and is checked in Figure 7.3; the memo’s criticism that σ is treated as known is the same point stated without the formula.

The extreme case. With σ′ chosen as ∞ the correction is zero and the corrected index is the matched one. The matched index is therefore the variety adjustment with the elasticity set to infinity, that is, with goods treated as perfect substitutes, which is the assumption under which losing a variety costs nothing.

7.3How much overlap is there?

How large the problem is depends on how much the two countries’ goods overlap. A natural measure is the number of common goods divided by the number of goods either country buys. Suppose each good is available in country j with probability qj and in country k with probability qk, independently. For a large number of goods the ratio of common to either is close to J(qj,qk)=qjqkqj+qk−qjqk. Figure 7.4 plots it. If both countries have the same availability q, the formula reduces to q/(2−q), which at q=0.8,0.6,0.4 gives 0.667, 0.429 and 0.250. The simulations below report mean overlaps of 67, 43 and 26 percent. The last differs because the design redraws any economy in which some pair shares fewer than three goods, which cuts off the low-overlap tail of the draws.

The surface says two things. Overlap falls fast as either country’s variety falls, and it is the lesser of the two countries that sets the limit, because J≤min(qj,qk). A rich country with every good and a poor country with half of them overlap on half; two countries with half each overlap on a third.

7.4Restriction maps with a number on them

Part I told the story in terms of stalks and restriction maps, and this chapter has the first real economic example in which two countries’ stalks differ. Country c holds its prices and shares for the goods in Gc. The edge from j to k carries data on the shared goods S. A restriction map takes what the country holds to what the edge holds.

The matched index uses the map that keeps the prices on S and renormalizes the shares on S to sum to one. That map is a projection, and it forgets one number: country c’s shares on S, before renormalizing, are the renormalized shares times λcjk. The factor λcjk is exactly what the projection discards. The corrected index uses a restriction map that also carries it, and on log price levels it acts as an additive shift by −log⁡λcjk/(σ−1). We can say it in the language of Chapter 4: it is a translation factor, one at each end of each edge, of the kind that let two parties with different frames agree after translation. The corrected index passes through that translation. Under identical tastes the translated data on every edge are differences of the same potential log⁡Pc, and the loop sums vanish.

That is the content of the section and also its limit. Projection is the wrong restriction map when goods differ, because it throws away information the comparison needs. The right one is only slightly richer. And the sheaf-theoretic language has so far contributed a name for something the index-number literature already does. The memo says the same: the reformulation would count as more than a restatement only if it delivered something the literature lacks, such as a test of which pairs’ variety terms are inconsistent or a rule for which bilateral comparisons to collect. We have not found either.

7.5What the papers say

What the paper says: Feenstra (1994), New product varieties and the measurement of international prices

This project holds the reference and its OpenAlex record, and no copy of the paper. There is no open copy we know of and we did not download it. We have not read it. All that we use is the form of the variety adjustment for one country between two dates, a ratio of spending shares on the goods available at both dates, raised to the power 1/(σ−1). We used it from memory and confirmed in simulation that, with the exact CES index as the target, the adjusted index recovers it. That check shows that the formula is right in the model of this chapter. It does not show what the paper assumes, how it estimates σ, or what its empirical results are, and we say nothing about them.

What the paper says: Handbury and Weinstein (2015), Goods prices and availability in cities

Handbury and Weinstein study barcode data for 49 U.S. cities and name two biases in comparisons of prices across places: heterogeneity bias, from comparing different goods, and variety bias, from ignoring goods that some places do not have. We read the published version selectively, Sections 2 to 6, after a first pass from a summary and after the first open copy we found turned out to be the 2011 NBER working paper, whose numbers can differ. Their variety adjustment uses national spending shares of the products available in each city, raised to the power 1/(1−σ); that is the λ factor of this chapter. As we read it, they compare each city with “the nation as a whole”, a star graph with no loops, so their index is transitive by construction and cannot register an inconsistency between two cities. We did not find a discussion of circularity, but we read selectively and cannot say none exists. The paper reports that the variety effect is large: about 110,000 grocery varieties in New York against under 24,000 in Des Moines, and a population elasticity of the price index that falls from 4.2 percent to 0.4 percent as the other corrections are added and turns to −1.1 percent when the variety correction is added last.

What the paper says: Biesel, McSwiggen, Theodosopoulos and Titelbaum (2025), Topological obstructions to shared priors

Each agent has a probability measure on the set of possibilities it is aware of, and agents may be aware of different sets. An ur-prior is one measure on the whole space whose conditional on each agent’s set is that agent’s measure. Their Theorem 4.1 says that, for pairwise compatible agents, the log ratio of two agents’ probabilities of their common event is a 1-cocycle, and a coboundary exactly when an ur-prior exists; Theorem 4.2 says pairwise checks suffice for every configuration if and only if the overlap complex has no first cohomology. We read pages 1 to 8 in full and the statements of the two theorems, not the cohomology background or the proofs. The match with this chapter is our own reading and not in the paper: a country’s shares over its goods are a probability measure on a set that differs by country, and log⁡λi−log⁡λj is their cocycle up to the factor 1/(σ−1). There is a caution. Their pairwise compatibility requires two agents to have the same relative probabilities on the common set. Under CES that holds for two countries only if bicpic1−σ is proportional across the two on the shared goods, which with identical tastes means equal relative prices there and fails generically when prices differ across countries, so their theorem does not apply as stated to the economy of this chapter. The identification has not been checked beyond that.

7.6What we found

The experiment

The earlier experiment of Chapter 6 gave every country every good, and the memo flagged that limitation. The third research cycle removed it (experiments/exp3_different_goods.py). Eight countries, forty goods, σ=4, log prices with standard deviation 0.3, a taste weight per good with a common component of standard deviation 0.5 and a country-specific component of standard deviation τ∈{0,0.2}. Each good is available in each country with probability q∈{1,0.8,0.6,0.4}, and any draw in which some pair shares fewer than three goods is redrawn. Two hundred economies per cell. Each pair is compared by the matched index and by the corrected index of equation (7.1). The entry is the share of the squared variation of the 28 indexes that does not glue, meaning the part outside the coboundaries.

Identical tastes Taste dispersion 0.2
q Mean overlap Matched Corrected Matched Corrected
1.0 100% 0.0% 0.0% 0.9% 0.9%
0.8 67% 19.4% 0.0% 19.1% 1.9%
0.6 43% 35.3% 0.0% 36.0% 2.9%
0.4 26% 49.1% 0.0% 46.8% 4.7%

The zeros are floating-point zeros: the corrected entries with identical tastes in the results file are of order 10−28 to 10−31, and the entry at q=1 is 2×10−27 for both indexes. In every draw the corrected index equaled the true difference in price levels plus the taste term on the common goods, with a largest gap of 3×10−13. Figure 7.5 draws the table.

One triangle, many draws

The table pools 21 independent loops. To see what one loop does we wrote a second script for this chapter, figures/ch07_loops.py, which is not one of the research experiments. It draws sixty triangles for each q in the same design, with three countries and identical tastes, and computes the loop sum IAB+IBC−IAC of each index in log points (Figure 7.6). The root mean square of the matched loop sum is 0.000 at q=1, 0.078 at 0.8, 0.124 at 0.6 and 0.295 at 0.4. The corrected loop sum is below 5×10−16 in every one of the 240 draws. The invented economy of the opening, with a loop sum of 0.978, lies beyond all of these, though not far beyond the largest, 0.857 at q=0.4. Its small size is part of the reason: the same script reruns its design, ten goods with three shared per pair, with 20,000 fresh draws of prices and tastes, and the matched loop sum there has a root mean square of 0.40. The draw itself is the rest, since only 1.7 percent of those draws reach 0.978.

Findings of the cycle

  1. When goods differ, the matched index fails circularity badly even with identical tastes: a fifth of its variation with two thirds overlap, half with a quarter overlap.

  2. The corrected index glues exactly under identical tastes, at every overlap.

  3. With taste differences, the corrected index’s obstruction is the taste term again, and it grows as overlap falls, from 0.9 to 4.7 percent.

  4. In the language of Part I, projection onto shared goods is the wrong restriction map; the right one carries the factor λ at each end of each edge, and under identical tastes those factors compose around every loop.

What was wrong along the way, and what limits this

The cycle started from a gap in the previous one. Its memo had said that its simulation used a common list of goods and that the case of differing goods, “the part of the sheaf framework that is not already index-number theory”, was not tested. The result is that the part is the variety adjustment of Feenstra and of Handbury and Weinstein: the cycle’s own verdict was that it confirms known economics and does not extend it.

Three corrections along the way belong in the record. The notes first called the variety formula used from memory, with the paper marked “to read”, and that is still the state of affairs for Feenstra. The first reading of Handbury and Weinstein was from a search summary, and the first open copy turned out to be a working paper, so we replaced it with the published version before using any of its numbers. And the mapping to Biesel and co-authors carries the caveat above, from reading the theorem’s hypotheses against the CES model, that their compatibility condition fails generically here.

The limits are the memo’s. The design uses one elasticity, treated as known, and the section above shows what a wrong one costs. The taste obstruction stays under five percent even at a quarter overlap, so it is small in this design. And the reformulation is so far a restatement: nothing in it tests which pairs’ variety terms are inconsistent or says which bilateral comparisons to collect. The concrete empirical design that came out of the reading is the one Handbury and Weinstein’s data would allow, computing city-pair indexes directly instead of city-to-nation and measuring the loop residual across 49 cities, and the data are restricted (Kilts Center), so that has not been done.
